utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber understands that the Prosecution would like to raise two matters. Now, they have been put on paper already. Perhaps you could cut it short, Mr. Weber. The first one is that in relation to P02521, where pages 6 and 7 of the English version were missing, that the Prosecution has now uploaded the complete English version under 65 ter number 30350(a) and that the B/C/S translation is correct as originally uploaded and has been attached to the number I just -- the document -- the number of it I just referred to, and that you had requested the Court Officer be instructed to replace the existing incomplete version with the complete one uploaded under that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, exactly what I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you are instructed to replace the existing incomplete version of P2521 by 65 ter number 30350(a). The other matter was a missing page 22 in relation to Exhibit P03228. We do understand that the Prosecution has meanwhile uploaded the complete English translation for this document under doc ID 0017-4125-1, and the Chamber understands that you would wish that the new complete English translation replaces the old one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you're hereby instructed to replace the existing incomplete English translation as uploaded for P03228 by a new complete translation which is doc ID 0017-4125-1. Could the usher escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not more than I asked for so I'll finish probably in the next 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, you say not more than you asked for. I do understand that you've used 34 minutes and you asked for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think I asked for an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our information is that you asked for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We sent an e-mail to the Prosecution and to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I may have missed that. We'll have a look at it and please meanwhile proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, good morning. Mr. Pejic, before we continue I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Lukic will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually before I continue I would just like to tender 1D3086 to be MFIed since it does not have English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Lukic, I can confirm that you did announce -- you didn't ask for more time but you said you would use more time. Okay, that's in your -- but you have informed us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D3086 receives number D592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just in relation to that document -- good morning, sorry, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone. At this point we do object to the admission of the document. I know counsel has just offered it in to MFI it until translation comes in. I do have some follow-up questions to the witness about the document, but it would be helpful at this point to know how the details that are provided in this list are probative. I'm still at a loss for how it's relevant to the allegations in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a brief response to that, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think Your Honour asked me yesterday. We think it directly goes towards mens rea of my client, since we heard from this witness that Mr. Mladic was privy with the patients of other nationalities treated in the -- this gentleman's hospital, that there was no any objection or order or instruction that Croats and Muslims were treated at that hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's not restart that. Certainly the Chamber will not engage in debate on that. Apparently, your position is that you cannot have mens rea one day and not -- you can have mens rea one day and not the other day. Well, that's a legal issue. Let's rather put a few questions and then let's later consider in more detail the relevance of the submissions and of the document. Madam Registrar, the document should be MFIed pending translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, I asked all the questions I had regarding this document, so if my learned friend wants to continue, I think the doctor is willing and able.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that will be done in cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We just shortly need D589 on our screens. It's the statement of this gentleman. And we need page 5, paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher will give a hard copy of the statement to the witness, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, in this paragraph you spoke about the shelling of the improvised bus station in October 1992, before the municipality of Ilidza, and you said that were you an eyewitness of this event. Could you please tell us, briefly, what it was that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was an eyewitness. Briefly, I was in the municipality building of Ilidza. I was seeking assistance to have the hospital removed to another building. When I was waiting to be received by someone there, a few shells fell in the immediate vicinity of the municipality. One of them fell about five metres away from the place where citizens were waiting for a bus, and somebody from that big group said, "There's the doctor in the municipality. Call him." And I went out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there? Mr. Lukic, to ask the witness what he saw, if there are 15 lines in his statement, what he saw is really asking for repetition. Please focus questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you notice in terms of the sequence of the falling of the shell?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see how the shells were falling, one after the other, all at once?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that but I heard them falling one after the other in very short intervals. And when the last shell fell and hit the target, then there was no more shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, intervals, are we talking about seconds or are we talking about minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, given this distance, it's very hard for me to say. Certainly it wasn't a long interval, say 10 to 15 seconds, up to one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll kindly ask to have 1D2828 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, as for this document, we also did not manage to obtain a translation because we got it from you only recently. Could you please just read out to us what it says on the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document has to do with the "shelling of a bus stop at the municipality of Ilidza on the 26th of October 1992. Civilian target. (At the intersection of the roads for Blazuj and Hrasnica. In front of the building of the municipality.)"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my signature and it is my facsimile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you treat these people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I treated those who were alive, and even those who unfortunately we did not manage to save. Most of the people who are on this list are people I knew personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I tender that into the evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd have exactly the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2828 receives number D593, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D593 is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And yesterday we were ordered to play that video with this witness just for identification, so I would kindly ask my colleague Mr. Ivetic to play for us D523 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, now a video is going to be shown for you and you should tell us briefly what it is that you see in this video and whether you recognise the site and the protagonists.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Today the medical personnel of the Blazuj hospital found two tanks with interesting contents among the oxygen tanks received as humanitarian aid. The oxygen tanks were opened in the presence of UNPROFOR representatives. Gunpowder was found in one of them while the other one was filled with mortar fuses. We are asking Dr. Pejic, how do these tanks end up in the hospital. Dr. Pejic: This is how they arrived. The police at the border crossing at Kobiljaca established that there were some oxygen tanks being transported to the Kosevo hospital or somewhere else, and, well, pursuant to some procedure they took out ten tanks to be delivered to this area here. Out of those ten, this hospital got five tanks. To our astonishment, well, we found out that two of the five tanks did not contain oxygen, that they were much heavier than the others. At first we thought it was water or something frozen, bearing in mind the cold weather. But even after it got warmer the tanks were as heavy as they had been before and then we decided to call the people who knew how to deal with that. They opened the tanks and found out that they contained gunpowder. Voice of the female reporter: We do not know how many shipments like this one have arrived in the hands of Muslim fighters through UNPROFOR under the motto humanity without borders, but we do not know how many missiles have been made from their contents, do we? But considering the fact that in the recent months all the Serbian positions around Sarajevo, especially those at Hadzici and Ilidza, have been he shelled with handmade missiles every day and that they are responsible for the deaths of many innocent civilians, especially children, we can say with certainty that a lot of such shipments have arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's only now that the translation was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I wasn't on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what this is all about. I can recognise, first of all, myself in this video footage and also some people who are wearing uniforms. These are oxygen tanks that we got from the UNHCR transport. This happened towards the end of 1992 and these two were opened in 1993, the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would like now this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, any objection to it now being admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number was? Let me just have a look. D523, which was MFIed, is hereby admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, what was the position? Did you talk to UNPROFOR representatives? Did they accept this involvement? Did they believe that they were involved or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk to them personally but I heard a conversation that the representatives of the police and the military had with them. If I understood it correctly, and as far as I can remember, representatives of UNPROFOR - I think it was the 5th Battalion of the French Legion - their statement was that they do not believe what we had presented. As a matter of fact, as far as I can remember, from the translation, they said that we had staged all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether the Serb side had staged this, rigged it? How were these tanks opened? How were attempts to that effect made, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the answer is absolutely not. The tanks were in the basement of the hospital. We tried to open them as usual in order to get oxygen through the valve. Nothing happened. We called the man who worked with oxygen and he opened this the way you're supposed to open it, and he informed us at the hospital what this was all about. All of this was done within the hospital and within the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. These were all the questions that we had at this moment for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Hasan, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Hasan. You'll find her to your right. Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Doctor, during the wartime period, you were the director of the Blazuj hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you just remind us of what your specialty is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a specialist for ear, throat and nose, and also for neck surgery.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did you treat patients at this hospital for -- for other conditions that they had, outside of your specialisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. From 1992 to 1996, we all behaved like war surgeons, that is to say there are no restrictions there, unless there is another doctor present there who was more competent to treat a disease. So we treated everyone, and I personally treated many conditions that would not fall within my own specialty, among other things serious injuries of the blood system, of the entire body, surgery of the eye, brain, amputations and so on and so forth, not to go into all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you've testified yesterday about your treatment of patients from various ethnicities. I'd just like to ask you about one particular patient. Do you recall someone by the name of Ramiz Mujkic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name of Ramiz Mujkic very well and I know him personally. After the war we met again. I am very pleased to say that the hospital that he was brought to saved his life, which shows that we did not treat people any differently on the basis of ethnicity. Rather, that we treated everyone the same way. I testified about Ramiz Mujkic in the proceedings against Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only question that was put to you, whether you knew the name, and wait for the next question by Ms. Hasan. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And doctor, he was brought to the Blazuj hospital in August 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if I can just pull up 65 ter 03758, and doctor, I believe you've seen -- you've seen this document before. And what it is is, as it comes up there, it's a certificate from the Blazuj hospital -- I don't have anything on the screen. Witness, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise this document, but I can see the contents and I can see that it was signed by the duty doctor. I don't know which doctor it was, because there is no stamp with a name, and there is no name typed up and this is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And doctor, you do remember it says here that it's a certification that Mr. Ramiz Mujkic was, on the orders of the Rajlovac Brigade military police and security officer Vlasto Apostolski, they took responsibility for the prisoner and escorted him to the Svrake military prison. You recall Ramiz Mujkic being brought and taken away by military police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't remember that because I was not in the hospital when he was taken away. I was in the hospital when he was brought in. Now, I really can't remember who brought him in. I suppose it was the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, doctor. And one of the injuries that Mr. Mujkic presented with was an injury to his leg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And do you recall, doctor, that his treating physician, I believe it was Dr. Popovic, had recommended that his leg be amputated, and you, as the chief, said instead that his leg should be saved and a fixator should be installed? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, we have information from Mr. Ramiz Mujkic, a statement from him that he was in the field, he had heard a burst of gunfire after which he was hit in the right thigh. He fired some rounds himself in the direction from where he was hit, and then after running out of ammunition, he decided to surrender and said, "Don't shoot. I'm Ramiz Mujkic." After which he was arrested and he was taken to the Rajlovac army barracks. While at the barracks, he was repeatedly beaten and he was beaten on the injury where he had been shot. So when he presented to the hospital, he was in bad shape; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that from the point of view of hygiene he was in a bad state. The wound to his right leg, if I recall correctly, was also in a very bad state, and that leg was broken in the thigh area. The thigh bone was broken.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just turn the page in this document and we'll see the letter of discharge. You see here that he was admitted on the 8th of August 1992 and then subsequently -- I believe we have the date of discharge on the 22nd of August 1992. Now, doctor, under the heading, "Diagnosis," we see that it reads, "Vulnera explosiva fermoris L-dex-fractura femoris L-dex," so he presented with, as I understand it, lacerated tissue, a lacerated wound, and a fracture to his right femur; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Would you say, doctor --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the right femur and he had an explosive wound in the right thigh area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in terms of -- in terms of this injury that he presented with, would you say that his diagnosis was consistent with him having been shot in his right femur and then beaten on the injury?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstand me or perhaps I did not understand you. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: My question is: The diagnosis recorded here on this document, is that consistent with what he says happened to him, that is that he was shot on his leg and then he was beaten on that injury?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that he gave to the Court, well, I did not see it. We had a lot of wounded people come in, and we did not go into details how the wounds were sustained. Based on the features of the wound, we were, for the most part, able to say whether it was a wound caused by an ordinary bullet, a fragmenting bullet, a wound injured by shell shrapnel, or a wound that was self-inflicted. In this case, it was a wound which was not inflicted immediately prior to his arrival to hospital. It was inflicted earlier. And this is the explanation for the status of this wounded person. The wound had been untreated, it was infected, and the wounded person himself was, in terms of hygiene, in a very bad state. Dr. Popovic, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. You are expanding on all kinds of causes apart from the one that was asked. The question was, the diagnosis as recorded here, whether that would be consistent with what that person had told, that is that he was shot in his leg and then beaten up on that injury, so not self-inflicted but beaten by whomever on that injury. Is what you read as the diagnosis consistent with that story, or does one contradict the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this letter of discharge, there is no information about any injuries caused by beatings or blows. The diagnosis "vulnera explosiva" means that the wound was caused by an explosive device. Now, as to the kind of explosive device that caused the injury, I cannot help you here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, I do want to follow up on the answer you previously gave which was you were talking about the specific situation of this -- of this individual, and I appreciate that now you have just given an answer generally. But with this specific Ramiz Mujkic, and you have pointed out that there was some time that elapsed from when he sustained his injury to when he came to the hospital, and you've mentioned the injury was infected and so on, so I'd like you to consider the specific circumstances of Ramiz. And if I'm telling you to accept or I'm telling you that he is saying that he was shot and then hit on that injury in addition to it being infected and so on, would that be consistent with a finding under the diagnosis that this was vulnera explosiva femoris, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to provide an explanation for my answer. You are asking me to give you a "yes" or "no" answer. How can I know?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir -- please continue. You can explain.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can you make a claim that he surrendered the very moment that he was injured? And how am I to know when he sustained his injury? And whether, indeed, he provided correct information. I'm just telling you the status, his status at the time when he was brought to the hospital and the condition of his wound because, I'm sorry, the doctor, the orthopaedic surgeon, who is more senior than I am, he is very experienced. He worked in the clinical centre, and he wanted to immediately amputate his leg above the wound, and I ordered that everything be done to save his leg, and his leg indeed was saved. Now, I really am not aware of any other information. You should ask those who had brought him in and those who held him there, who kept him under guard while he was there. Mr. Mujkic may have been wounded and may have stayed on his own before surrendering for a while and then surrendered only at the later stage. He may have been beaten. I don't know. I can't tell you. And I can neither confirm nor deny. I cannot give you a "yes" or "no" answer to your question. I am simply telling you, I'm testifying as to the condition he was in when he was brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question? Doctor, you say you saw the patient when he arrived at hospital. Now, the condition in which you found him, would you say his injury was consistent with his leg being shot at and then being beaten on the injury? I'm not asking you about this report. I'm asking you about what you observed on him when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already answered this question. Neither I nor the doctor who treated him saw the -- any wounds inflicted by blows or beating. The wound was infected and it takes a while for the wound to get infected from the moment the wound is inflicted until the moment this person is brought to the hospital with this infection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question really is did the wound look like it was just caused by the shooting or did it show that this was further tampering with it after the shooting? That you should be able to notice if you look at the witness. And therefore you're able to give a professional opinion as to what the injury is consistent with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was an explosive wound. In other words, it was not a gunshot wound. And this wound was infected. That's all I can tell you as to this man. And we really were not able to ascertain, and we did not enter any such information into this letter of discharge, whether there were any other injuries. We did not ascertain any other injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one very short question. Would you agree with me that in this letter of discharge, where findings and opinion are described, that nothing is said about the wound not being fresh and being badly infected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would agree with you that it does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Doctor, we see on this document that you've -- your name on the right, the right-hand side; is that correct? You signed off on this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not sign this. My name is indeed here. It's printed. You have seen my signature on other documents. On that day, obviously I was not in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, doctor. I'm just going to move on to the -- the 1993 list we were looking at yesterday. And this is a -- this is a list you said, doctor, that -- it's D590 -- sorry, D590 is not the one. It's 65 ter 1D03086, D592 MFI. And according to your testimony, there are at least in part some members recorded here who were members of the HVO. Are you aware of any conflicts between the HVO and the ABiH that took place in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall roughly when that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was June 1993, or perhaps early July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that this document was created by a specialist service in the hospital and you said it was created in 1994 and that you signed it and that it was sent to the ministry, the RS Ministry of Health. What's the specialist service in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specialist service does not produce these documents. It's the administration that does it, assisted by the doctors, those who are available. Probably more than one doctor provided the diagnosis in Latin. I'm sorry, yes. The diagnoses are all copied from the protocol book.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the purpose of this list was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list was made at the request of the Ministry of Health of Republika Srpska, because they kept records of all the civilian casualties and, indeed, all the other casualties of war. There was a special department, an institution, in fact, that processed statistical data about all the persons injured and who were sick during the war, and they had separate records for soldiers and for civilians. This institution was called -- I think it was the Institute of Public Health, if I'm not mistaken, and it was part of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you explain why, on this list, the protocol numbers start - and we can turn to this, if need be - it starts at protocol number 32 and jumps to protocol number 68 and then protocol number 85? So can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The first protocol every year is protocol number 1, but those protocols do not list soldiers, military personnel, members of the Republika Srpska army, and also you don't list those who only came in to have their dressings changed and those who were ill. So we did not have separate protocols for the wounded. We had hospital protocols, and you entered all those who came to seek medical assistance by number. And that is why the numbers are not consequential because other people, sick people, wounded people, are entered under the missing numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've taken a look at this document, and we've asked some people questions who are familiar with the wartime period, and we don't ordinarily see documents that look like this and what I mean by that, documents that are printed in this way, have a table like this, and have the type of font that's on this document. Can you tell us, you know, what equipment you had and what processing programmes were used to create this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't. I don't want to make a mistake. I don't know which people who are in a position to look at those lists. I would like to know who they were. And there are people who do programmes. I don't know whether this was done in Excel or in Word, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And the hospital retains the digital version of this original file?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this hospital closed down in 1996. It no longer exists, Madam. So there are protocols, and there is something that I had saved on the floppy disk, and I loaded it in the computer in the hospital where I worked up until a month ago, and this computer is in my possession. This was my personal computer. And the protocols that can be verified are available, as I have already told you, in the eastern new Sarajevo municipality, in the headquarters of an NGO, the Association of the Inhabitants of Ilidza and Friends of Ilidza, in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, do you know if any of the Muslims that were treated at your hospital and that you claim are on this list were brought to or taken from VRS-run labour camps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it was a run by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, that they came from or were taken to labour camps. Let's just leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness asked whether you are talking about labour camps run by the VRS or apparently he would like to know --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of any other labour camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, your question is very general. I don't know what area you're talking about. I know about the camp in Tarcin, in Silos, I know about the camps in Sarajevo, and -- well, probably there were camps on the Serb side, but I really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan has explained that she indeed referred to camps on the Serb side, run by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the Republika Srpska army did not run any camps. If there were any camps - I don't know what else to call them; I should call them prisons - they were run by another institution. I don't want to be wrong. You probably know more about that than I do. I don't know whether they were run by the police or by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just. You say there were no -- oh, yes, the army did not run any camps. You said there must have been others. But are you familiar with any of those camps run by Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was not in any of those camps, but I do know that some people were wounded as members or rather people who were under the compulsory work service. Now, where they were taken to do their work, what happened to them, how they were brought back, I really don't want to go into that because I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know about camps run by Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we mentioned the camp where Mr. Mujkic was. It was mentioned in the document pertaining to him but I don't know about that. I'm sure that the prisoners, the captives, were held somewhere. Now, whether it was in the Kula prison or somewhere else, I really can't tell you. We heard when we talked about Mr. Mujkic, we heard that he said that he was in the Gravaca concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he taken over by a VRS officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean Mr. Mujkic? Well, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the document says, what you just looked at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the document states the name of the person who took him over, and he signed this document because that's what we requested, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall the person's name but it's on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for the break. Mr. Pejic, we would take a break of 20 minutes and we would like to see you back after the break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, doctor, I'm just going to go back to one of the topics we discussed, after having reviewed your evidence on that, so I'm going to just ask you a couple more questions about this -- the patient Ramiz Mujkic. So if there is a situation where a patient presents themselves some days after the injury -- an injury was inflicted to them, their injury is swollen and infected, they arrive at your hospital, okay, are you able to tell -- I mean, you can't tell what the cause of that injury was, that presents itself to you in that shape; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are not forensic experts. We rely on what the patient tells us, and also what the wound looks like. So every wound has its own characteristics. As for this gentleman, this was an explosive wound. It was dirty, infected. Also, the bone was fractured. Therefore, I cannot give you more information because I don't have any more information.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And sir, when you say, okay, this was an explosive wound, are you describing the state of the wound, meaning the tissue as being lacerated, or are you talking about that this wound is -- you're making a determination as to an explosion occurring outside the body when you're using that Latin phrase?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An explosive wound is an open wound. It doesn't have a point of entry and a point of exit. Whereas a wound that is inflicted by a rifle bullet has its point of entry and point of exit. This was an open wound, quite simply as if you had cut the skin and the muscle. And not to provide an inadequate explanation. This is a wound that doesn't have a point of entry and a point of exit, from a projectile or air blast. So it's a projectile. It can be shrapnel or it can be a bullet. I don't know if I'm being clear enough. So every wound that hits a person, a gunshot wound, say, hits a person in a chest -- in his chest, there is no -- there can be a point of entry and a point of exit, whereas here it was the -- it was just hit in a single place and then it was infected. It was with dirty. The bone was fractured. We don't know how or when. Otherwise, all war wounds are not primarily sewn up. They are left open in order to control the infection and then ultimately they are stitched so that the wound can heal completely. As for gunshot wounds, they have their own canal that has to be left open. It has to be cleaned too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So, witness, if I understand you correctly, it's fair to say that, at least in these circumstances that we have been talking about, where there is an infected wound and so on, it's an open wound, the Latin phrase vulnera explosiva is a description of the injury that you see as -- on the patient?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. So the way the wound looks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd offer 65 ter 03758 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03758 receives number P6689, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6689 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to move on to briefly the incident involving the oxygen tanks, the one we just viewed on the video and that you've given evidence about in your statement. Now, in your statement at paragraph 24, you provide that the Serb side managed to arrange with UNHCR officials that a few of the needed oxygen tanks be taken out of the batch that was travelling to Sarajevo, and we can put up -- we can see that in your statement at paragraph 24. You see that in the second-to-last -- 24, near the end, "Since our hospital needed oxygen representatives of the Serb side managed to arrange with the UNHCR officials that a few of the much-needed oxygen tanks be taken out of the batch that would travel to Sarajevo." Who are you referring to when you say "the Serb side," representatives of the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Serb side, there was an office that dealt with UNHCR-related matters. It was in Rajlovac. The aid that arrived in Sarajevo, according to some agreement from the Serb side, that is to say all levels of government and those who were in charge of communicating with the UNHCR, bearing in mind the fact that we as a hospital needed oxygen, and certain contingents were sent to Sarajevo, what was agreed upon was a certain principle of allocation. I've already explained that. According to this principle, we were entitled to five tanks. Who agreed on this? Who signed this? On what conditions? I don't know. I've never seen that document but I know that it was based on some agreement. Because it's not only -- I mean this time it was gunpowder, but I know that during the war that crude oil was also brought in that way and then also food, humanitarian aid. There was also allocation of that. So that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you involved in that agreement that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's turn to 65 ter 1D00231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, may I ask you one question? You just talked about not only gunpowder, but also crude oil that was brought in that way. Did you see that with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see oil that way but that is how I received it in the hospital, because we had a laundry in the hospital, we had generators, and we got certain amounts of oil on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, doctor, what you're saying is that you did receive some oil, for example, and other supplies, from UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the office that received that, that was on the Serb side, and then they delivered this oil, this fuel, to us. Probably to the hospital in Kasindol as well, and other institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So the document that appears is not the one I want. If we could have 1D02031. What you see here, doctor, is the RS MUP report on the incident you talk about, and it's dated 2nd of February 1993. We can turn to page 2, please. Now, in this report, the Serbian public security station reports that you informed them of these two cylinders which were taken over from the UNHCR, that they did not contain gas. This is what you told them. And then continuing about halfway down the page, you see it says: "Following checks it was established that on 20 November 1992, the UNHCR representatives picked up 100 cylinders which were supposed to contain laughing gas from the Kovena enterprise in Visoko for the needs of the Kosevo hospital." And then just one paragraph below that: "While inspecting UNHCR vehicles at the Mostar intersection, officials of the Blazuj police station decided to take five cylinders and give them to the Blazuj military hospital." Okay? So, sir, according to the MUP, which has produced this report, there is no mention of any agreement about this, that, in fact, the police at that check-point decided to take the five cylinders from -- from the UNHCR convoy that was passing through. Now, that's not consistent to what -- with what you've told us today, that this arrived at your hospital pursuant to some agreement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're right on one point. I do know that this was an agreement. This was written by the commander of the police station, and I, as director, was informed that we would receive oxygen tanks because we needed oxygen to save people's lives, the lives of patients, the wounded, children. There was a children's department, too, in the hospital where children were being treated from their date of birth until the point when they were no longer children. I don't have a document in writing. I never received it. I just heard this from people who worked at this office in Rajlovac. Madam, different agreements were reached there. Different agreements. We were just the ones to whom this was delivered. And I know that it was the UNHCR that transported that. It wasn't Milan Pejic or Marko Markovic; it was UNHCR trucks that went to Sarajevo every morning with different cargo - sand, tanks. They were covered and some of the cargo could not be seen, and this time we got these oxygen tanks. Why would Visoko fill them with oxygen? They manufacture completely different things and -- may I just finish my sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You can finish your sentence if it's short.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All detonators were wrapped in Kovina Visoko paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: These agreements you heard about, you weren't involved in any of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2031 receives number P6690, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6690 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, doctor, you were never mobilised into the army, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You saw what I looked like when I was examining these oxygen tanks. I was wearing civilian clothing. I was supposed to be at the military hospital Zica in Blazuj and that was my assignment given to me by the municipal organ for National Defence. It wasn't mobilisation in the actual sense of the word but it did mean that I should be involved in the organisation of one segment of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But you were not a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very hard to say who was a soldier in war and who was not. I was assigned there. I had my work obligation at the Zica hospital in Blazuj. Later on, from the army, I received an assignment to be chief of the medical unit in a brigade because another doctor was supposed to be at the Zica hospital instead of me. According to this document, which is called VOB 8, according to which one part of the military -- of the hospital of Zica was mobilised from a military point of view and the other part of the hospital, Ivan Brigade, and I actually never did that because this work was being carried out by another person.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. You don't have any personal knowledge yourself about any orders or directions relating to attacks against Bosnian-controlled territory in Sarajevo, do you? I'm asking for your personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any personal knowledge. As a matter of fact, I didn't have any knowledge about attacks against our side, that is to say we were always caught by surprise. Many wounded persons were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you have any personal knowledge, again, about the sniping and shelling of civilians in Sarajevo and the injuries that those people sustained as a result of that during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowledge about sniping and shelling, about the sniping and shelling of Sarajevo? I don't have any personal knowledge about that, but I know about the sniping and shelling carried out against Serb civilians in the Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Doctor, are you aware, then, and I'm now not talking about your personal knowledge, are you aware that there were -- there was shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see that on TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you knew that was happening in Bosnian-held areas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw that on television, that is to say, I did not see it personally. I was not present there. And I cannot confirm that that happened and that it came from the Serb side. Also, I cannot deny it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you were asked yesterday about General Mladic, and you gave evidence that he visited the Blazuj hospital several times. Can you tell us when he visited your hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really did not keep records. It was a few times, three or four times, I believe. It was in 1993, and later. I know that it -- one of those occasions happened at the height of the Muslim-Croat conflict, when we had the largest number of Croatian injured in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you said "and later." You said he visited the hospital several times in 1993 and later. Did he visit the hospital in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. You're asking me about something of which I did not keep any records. I know that he visited the hospital three, maybe four times. I'm sure that he visited the hospital three times. He did not come to see the director and the hospital. He came to see the injured people, the sick people. He said hello to them. He shook hands with them. He wished them speedy recovery, his best wishes. This is all I know about his visits to the Blazuj hospital. He did not stay there long. These were just short visits.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I just want to know because you said that he visited the hospital after 1993 so I want to know did he visit the hospital in 1994, did he visit the hospital in 1995? Was it one time? Was it several times? Just give me the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already told you. It was in 1993, when we had the largest number of Croatian patients, soldiers or civilians, mostly civilians who lived in the HVO-controlled area, and this is all I can remember. I remember that he made a statement to the Republika Srpska TV in my office, and after that we just toured the hospital. We visited the wounded. I don't know about other visits. He may have visited the hospital when I was not there, but I really did not keep record of that. And it would be too much to ask from me to give you dates and how many times and what happened after 20 years. I really don't know. But I do know that he visited the hospital two, three or maybe more than three times but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, when he visited the hospital and you received him there, how did he arrive?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By car, in a Kampanjola car. It's an all-terrain vehicle, a jeep. I really don't know. I saw him in the hospital itself, once he entered. I did not welcome him in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. Any further questions, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I might have a few, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asked today about the wounding of Mr. Ramiz Mujkic. You were -- it was put to you that Mr. Mujkic said that a doctor recommended that his leg be amputated and that you insisted that fixators be put and that the leg be saved. At that time were there situations where there were discussions about whether a Serb soldier was discussed in the same terms, in other words, whether his leg should be amputated or saved? Do you remember having any such discussions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in such situations where you receive a wounded person with life-threatening injuries, and if the amputation of an limb would make it possible to save that person's life, then we amputated. In this case, this was not life-threatening. There was a risk to the leg, but whenever we could save a leg or a limb, regardless of the ethnicity of the patient, a Serb, Muslim or a Croat, we tried to save the leg because it is better to have a leg which does not look very good, which looks like a stick, than not to have a leg at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, just very briefly, the difference between wartime and peacetime surgery?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A huge difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard from you that although you are a specialist for ear, nose and throat surgery, that you performed other kinds of surgery, that you had to amputate limbs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I studied in medical school, we had a course in wartime surgery and we had to pass an exam.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us very briefly look at P6689. It's the letter of discharge for Mr. Mujkic. I need the last page of this document. I don't know how it was uploaded. We can see here from this document that this gentleman was received on the 8th of August 1992 and that he was discharged on the 22nd of August 1992. And we can see that he was discharged in a good condition. In the English version you can see this. It's written in capital letters. I know that you were not there in the hospital at the time of his discharge, but you said that you met this gentleman after the war.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he complain to you that he had been discharged from the hospital and that he had not been treated well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Quite the contrary. He was quite positive about his stay in our hospital. And if you allow me, we in fact had lunch when we met in the presence of his sister, and he told me many details. I don't recall those details now, but he was very positive about his stay in the hospital, and according to him, we treated him -- he was treated like any other patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions about the medical treatment of patients from other ethnic groups in your hospital. Did you have any problems? Did armed Serbs, civilians, cause you any problems because you were treating from other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were cases when family members or relatives of those who had been killed, who had been brought to the hospital and the ones that we couldn't save, wanted to exact revenge on the Muslims, and we had to respond very quickly. We, the medical workers, we had to take off their uniforms, we had to call the command, to make sure that those people were protected. In fact, some Muslims who were wounded on the front-line, we would register them under Serb names. Let me give you an example. There was a BH Army soldier whose last name was Pustahija. This is a very striking name. He was wounded on the Nisici plateau. He was very important for the army because he had a notepad with some codes. And many civilians were killed on that part of the battlefield, and they wanted to exact revenge. So we stabilised him once he reached the hospital, and in order to keep him safe, we registered him under a different name, and then we moved him out because we wanted to protect him against the bereaved relatives of those who had been killed and who wanted to get some revenge. Of course, people react to loss in different ways but there were also other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Interpreter's note: We did not interpret the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question to start with, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was not recorded. Let me repeat it. Were there any attacks on you personally because you provided medical treatment to people from other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no physical assaults, but verbal abuse, yes. Well, if I may, war is an abnormal situation, and all the bad things come up to the surface, and that goes for human nature, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you very much. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, a document was shown to you earlier, a report about what you called the issue with the oxygen tanks. Could I first ask you, were you there when these five tanks were received?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I could not be in the hospital for four years, 24 hours a day. So I was not there, probably I was not there when the oxygen tanks were -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to justify your absence. I'm just asking a simple question. So you were not there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it you who reported your doubts, your suspicions, about the oxygen tank?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not right away. If I may be allowed to explain? In hospital -- just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pejic, please answer my questions. So you say -- my question simply was, was it you? Was it you or was it someone else? Time may come later.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who notified the police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, but it was two months later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will be my next question, Mr. Pejic. What happened exactly? You said they were stored in the basement, these tanks, and at what point in time were you -- did you become aware of any suspicion about its content?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we received those tanks, they were stored in a part of the building, the part of the building where, before the war, there was the road maintenance unit that was in charge of maintaining roads in Sarajevo. Two of the tanks were much heavier than the other tanks, and the technicians who handled those tanks, which are used for the purpose of anaesthesia, they opened the tanks and no gas came out. One of the people in the maintenance section, they wanted to heat up the valves. They were mechanics. And well, fortunately they did not do it. We just set them aside and we simply waited for somebody who knows how to handle oxygen tanks to come. In the meantime, the Rajlovac facility where oxygen tanks could be filled became operational, and the person in charge of the facility came to the hospital, offered us the oxygen tanks from his facility, and I asked this person to examine the two tanks. There was attack on the Serb front-lines and I was in the surgery room, in the operating room. And at one point, one man rushed into the OR shouting, "Doctor, gunpowder." And I shouted at this man, I said, "You cannot enter the operation room like that because you're dirty." And he said that some gunpowder poured out of the tank when it was opened, and he told me that he could not get anything to come out of the other tank although the valve was opened. And I suggested that he should open the tank from the bottom, and he said that it was impossible to cut the tank in order to screw off the bottom of the tank and to then screw it closed again. He said it was impossible, to the best of his knowledge. At one point he came back into the hospital and he said, "Shell detonators," and after that, now that I knew what this was all about, I reported this incident to the military -- to the military, and the police, and they then informed the UNHCR. And that's it. And fortunately we did not heat up the tanks because people would die. There would be an explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, two questions. First question, when was UNPROFOR involved in this whole exercise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which exercise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was UNPROFOR at any time involved? Yes? After you had reported this to the police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR came with the police and the representatives of the Republika Srpska army to check, and of course the media were also there to check what was in those tanks. Not before that. Not with regard to the tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the report we saw, that is the report on television, it was said that the oxygen tanks were opened in the presence of UNPROFOR representatives, but on the basis of your testimony, I have to understand that they were opened again on the basis of -- in the presence of UNPROFOR because they had been opened already, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. How else could we tell that they were full of gunpowder if we had not opened them? And how else would we be able to tell they were full of detonators if we had not opened them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do not doubt that, but it was presented in a different way in this footage.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This gentleman, he returned the gunpowder and the detonator into the tanks, didn't take all of them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said, "I called the international observers of UNPROFOR to see for themselves what was there so that we could open the oxygen tanks in the presence of UNPROFOR and verify their content." Again, this is reopening it where they had been opened before? Perhaps I'm reading from the -- let me just see. No, that was in your old statement, and while your statement -- we received a new one, and the new one -- yes. So I don't take you back to that statement. Now, do you have any explanation why the report we just had a look at is consistently talking not about oxygen tanks but about tanks of laughing gas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is this laughing gas? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Laughing gas is N2O, if I may describe it in --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That is nitrogen oxide. No, no, no. This was oxygen. Sorry, I really don't know who wrote this, "laughing gas." Not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's consistently referred to as that you were given this nitrogen oxide, not that you were given oxygen.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see where that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read from you from the report which was admitted into evidence. It says -- let me see. "While inspecting UNHCR vehicles at the Mostar intersection, officials of the Blazuj police station decided to take five cylinders and give them to the Blazuj military hospital." Your hospital was a military hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a question, yes, in the middle of a quote.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a mixed hospital, both military and civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we find that in your statement, that you were partly military hospital, partly -- I'm a bit confused because we received two statements. The first one -- Mr. Lukic, anywhere, any mentioning of the military or half military character of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that I couldn't find it in the statement. That's why I started questioning of this document with this line of questions when I clarified what kind of hospital that was because it was not clear to me at the beginning either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of direct examination, I tried to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In proofing you were unable to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the proofing, I learned -- actually, we did discuss -- discussed it but I still wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, so that is how they -- I continue to read: "... decided to take five cylinders and give them to the Blazuj military hospital, expecting that they contained laughing gas needed for medical treatment." And earlier in that same report, we read: "Following checks, it was established that on the 20th of November 1992, the UNHCR representatives picked up 100 cylinders which were supposed to contain laughing gas, nitro oxygen, from the Kovina enterprise in Visoko for the needs of the Kosevo hospital." Do you have any -- I could show it to you. It's -- let me just.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation why the investigation is constantly talking about laughing gas and that you are talking about oxygen because you wouldn't use it for the same, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. But if you allow me, also, there is no reference to gunpowder or detonators in this report of UNPROFOR, and they were present in the tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pejic, if you were always jumping to conclusions so easily, then that is of some concern to me because the last line of this report reads, "The gunpowder and fuses that were found were taken by members of the Igman Brigade." So therefore if you say, "Well, this report doesn't even mention the fuses," that's just not accurate, unless you disagree. It's the last page, it's page 3 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry -- there is a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what would we then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the original, it says -- it's very hard to see, "oksid" something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but nitro oxygen, of course, also contains part of the word "oxygen".

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It should be nitro oxygen. In B/C/S it says only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second page in B/C/S. Could we have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fourth, paragraph, if somebody can read it, I really cannot. It's fourth paragraph, fourth line in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see what we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: P6690, I think is the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said he saw it so therefore I thought it would be on his screen. Yes, then we need the second page. And we need the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Second-last paragraph, the big one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I was referring to the third paragraph in the original, a short one. Could we zoom in on that? I'd rather zoom in in the original, the third paragraph. No, we are missing the relevant part. Let's have a look. Could we further zoom in on that same -- on that further higher, in the B/C/S, yes, that portion, yes, could we zoom in further? Mr. Lukic, I have great difficulties. I would like to have a more -- let me just try -- where do you see the word "oxygen," Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but in this paragraph, because in the translation, it says "laughing gas."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the paragraph I'm referring to, laughing gas is mentioned. Can you see that or is there a translation issue there as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next -- what I checked was the next paragraph in English as well. It says "laughing gas"; in B/C/S it said "oksid" and something, and in this paragraph I cannot read what it says in B/C/S really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you assist us? One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The paragraph in which you were able to read "oxygen" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apparently is the paragraph which starts with -- the second word looks like "Stanici" or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fourth line in the middle. "Nalazi oksid."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. In the fourth line there, you said, and there you read.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Oksid koji," "oxygen which."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Ms. Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. We are happy to send this for a review of the translation. It's difficult to read. Perhaps they can do so. And it's a CLSS translation, so I'm sure they can review it and verify what in fact it says. As far as we are concerned, we don't dispute that they were oxygen bottles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, if that's not in dispute, then I -- well, you present evidence which says it's laughing gas, and perhaps you were not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did see that it says laughing gas, in fact I think I even read that portion out. Whether it's a mistake in the translation or in fact they thought it was laughing gas, we have seen the UNPROFOR report as well which refers to them as oxygen cylinders. But we are happy to try and help to resolve this by getting the translation verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I immediately refrain, if there is no dispute about it between the parties. But I was confused by presenting evidence that it's laughing gas where other evidence also presented by the Prosecution says it's oxygen. Okay, I leave that apart. And Judge Moloto has a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doctor, did I understand your evidence correctly that it was some time after the tanks were in the hospital that somebody discovered that some were heavier than the others and that's what caused the suspicion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not understand this properly. We noticed immediately that they were heavier than the other ones; however, we thought that there was more oxygen in them because every tank that has oxygen in it is opened in one direction, but one containing laughing gas is opened in another direction. So one cannot confuse the two. Please allow me to finish my sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to just clarify it. So when you say you discovered immediately the difference in weight, was it on the day when you received the tanks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discovered that they were heavier and that they were not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me what happened 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. I want to know --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately or the following day, I don't know, the moment when we needed oxygen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doctor, you're here to testify about what happened years ago, and you're telling us you remember some things very clearly. Now, I'm asking you about something that happened 20 years ago. Simply, the question is did you discover the difference in weight on the day you received the tanks or sometime later? And you say I didn't understand you. I want to understand you. When did you discover?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discovered the difference in weight the day when we got them from the truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then you kept them for two months before you opened them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When a tank is used up, then another one follows. When the technicians took the heavy tank, they didn't get this gas from it and then we decided to open the other one using the valve. We didn't get it then either. So we left it in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When a tank gets finished and another one is used, were they opened the same day? Did one get finished the same day and you opened the next one that you found to be heavy?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you discovered this was heavier, this was sometime after receipt?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. We opened -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, my problem is on the day they were received, I'm sure there was still a difference in weight and I'm surprised that on that day, the suspicion did not arise. It only arises when you opened the subsequent bottle sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you've understood what I said. The tank is put on the apparatus when oxygen is needed. We cannot use all five tanks at the same time, using the same equipment. Since these are large tanks, industrial-sized ones, there was more oxygen in them than in the medical tanks. Once one tank is used, then the other one is used. When the turn of these tanks came, I really don't know. But when we realised that the gas was not coming out of them, we left them in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the point I'm making. That's just -- I understood you very clearly. Now I'm saying when these tanks arrived, whoever received them should have felt -- discovered the difference in weight. But then the weight is being discovered when you opened the subsequent one, which is after some time that they have been in your storage. Now, I'm saying, isn't it surprising that the weight was not discovered earlier, the difference in weight was not discovered earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not correct. The weight, the difference in weight, was discovered immediately, as soon as they were taken off the truck. The technician's explanation as to why they did not attach the heavy tank is because they were keeping it for later, because they thought that it contained more gas than the other tanks. That was the only explanation that I received from them. This is the only explanation I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Can I ask you something else on a different point? At page 20 of today's transcript, lines 18 to 24, you say, amongst other things, "As far as I know, the Republika Srpska army did not run any camps." We were talking about labour camps here. You have testified that you were working as a doctor and you were never in the field. How do you know that the VRS army did not have labour camps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not state that categorically. I said, "as far as I know." So these are two different things. I did not make this claim. But it was logical that you should -- if you have prisoners, you have to keep them somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, you are very right. You said as far as you know, and I'm asking you the question, as far as you know, how did you know that the VRS didn't have labour camps? I still ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you willing to accept the claim that is based on what I heard from the media? Or are you willing to accept those things that I saw and that I know? I learned from the media --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you didn't say in your evidence you learned it from the media. You said as far as you know. That's what you said. If you had said from the media and you said you had heard it from the media that would be different. I wouldn't be asking you these questions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC [Resumed]
